nodes.title: Generate register-map (Tier 1)
nodes.prompt:
You are encoding an STM32 microcontroller into the OpenDatasheet part format. This is the STRUCTURAL step: produce a complete, registered-precise register-map (Tier 1) with provenance on every leaf.

INPUTS — read the manifest first:
  cat datasheets/{{chip}}/chip.json
It gives: mpn, family, packages, revision, `out` (where the part JSON must land), `svd` filename, reference_manual {doc, rev, pdf, toc_pages, url}, datasheet {doc, rev, pdf}.

READ THE PROJECT'S OWN GUIDE before doing anything else — it is the source of truth for this pipeline:
  cat tools/ADDING-A-CHIP.md
Also skim a known-good chip module for the exact shape to mirror:
  sed -n '1,60p' tools/chips/stm32g474.py

STEPS (follow ADDING-A-CHIP.md; commands are relative to the repo root, which is your cwd):
1. Copy the template module and the SVD into the toolchain:
     cp tools/chips/stm32g474.py tools/chips/{{chip}}.py
     cp datasheets/{{chip}}/<svd-from-manifest> tools/chips/{{chip}}.svd
2. Sanity-check the SVD parses (note the register NAMING convention you see — e.g. are register names prefixed like `RCC_CR`, or bare like `CR`? this affects section mapping):
     python3 tools/svd2od.py tools/chips/{{chip}}.svd RCC | head -40
3. Build the provenance section map from the reference manual. THIS RM's table of contents is long — use the manifest's `toc_pages` value (do NOT rely on the default 72):
     python3 tools/make_sections.py datasheets/{{chip}}/<rm-pdf> tools/chips/{{chip}}.sections.json --toc-pages <toc_pages-from-manifest>
   Confirm it produced hundreds of keys: python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('tools/chips/{{chip}}.sections.json'));print(len(d),'keys'); print([k for k in d if 'RCC' in k][:6])"
4. Edit tools/chips/{{chip}}.py descriptor from the manifest: ID, SVD_FILE, SECTIONS_FILE, OUT (= manifest `out`), EMIT_ALL=True, DOC_RM (= reference_manual.doc), RM_REV (= reference_manual.rev), PART (mpn/manufacturer/family/revision/lifecycle/packages), DOCUMENTS (one entry per the manifest's reference_manual AND datasheet — id/kind/rev/url). Set TIERS=[1] for now.
   CRITICAL: the template is the STM32G474 module — it is full of G474-SPECIFIC curation that is WRONG for this chip. You MUST strip it to a clean auto-mode baseline before building: set PERIPHERALS=[], AUTO_PREFIX_OVERRIDE={}, CHAPTER_FALLBACK={}, ACCESS_FIX={}, EXTRA_PERIPHERALS=[], and remove/blank the G474 LIMITS/ELECTRICAL and the hand-written enum/peripheral dicts (EN_*, GPIO/RCC/USART/... spec dicts). Do not let G474 register names, enums, or access values leak into this chip. Keep only the generic auto-mode machinery (CLEAR_SUFFIX="ICR", CLEAR_NAMES={"SCR","IFCR"}) and the build helpers the module needs.
5. First build and READ THE STDERR COVERAGE REPORT:
     python3 tools/build.py {{chip}}
   It prints: N peripherals, M registers, and provenance: X register-precise, Y chapter-level, Z TBD.
6. DRIVE `TBD` TO 0. For each peripheral still TBD or chapter-level, reason about WHY its registers didn't resolve to a section, then fix with the smallest mechanism (per ADDING-A-CHIP.md §"close provenance gaps"):
     - AUTO_PREFIX_OVERRIDE: when the SVD peripheral base (e.g. SPI1) differs from the RM's generic TOC placeholder (e.g. SPIx) — map "SPI":"SPIx", "GPIO":"GPIOx", "TIM":"TIMx" as needed. Inspect the sections.json keys to learn the placeholders.
     - CHAPTER_FALLBACK: when the RM documents the peripheral only at chapter granularity (no per-register TOC entry) — map the prefix to its chapter number (find it in the sections.json or via the RM).
     - A curated section_map on a per-peripheral spec for collisions.
   Rebuild after each change; the TBD count must drop. Iterate until `0 TBD`.
7. FIX STATUS/CLEAR REGISTER ACCESS. The SVD mis-types write-1-to-clear/read-clear registers as plain read-write. For the interrupt/status registers of the main peripherals, verify the real access in the RM:
     python3 tools/rm_inspect.py datasheets/{{chip}}/<rm-pdf> ADC_ISR
   (it prints access tokens -> schema access). Encode the corrections in ACCESS_FIX, e.g. {"ADC":{"ISR":"w1c"}, "EXTI":{"PR1":"w1c"}}. Check at least: ADC ISR, EXTI pending, any *ICR/*SCR/*IFCR (the CLEAR_SUFFIX/CLEAR_NAMES rule should already handle most clear registers — confirm).
SECURE-WORLD ALIASES (TrustZone parts — STM32U5/L5/H5). If the SVD exposes every peripheral a SECOND time as a `SEC_<name>` duplicate with identical registers (just the secure address space) — and the manifest sets `drop_secure_aliases: true` — DROP the duplicates: set `SKIP_PREFIXES = ("SEC_",)` in tools/chips/{{chip}}.py (build.py honors it in auto-mode AND in curated `emit` lists). Do NOT add any `SEC_` instance to a curated peripheral's `emit` list. After building, confirm zero remain: `python3 -c "import json;d=json.load(open('<out>'));print(sum(1 for p in d['profiles']['register-map']['peripherals'] if p['name'].startswith('SEC_')),'SEC_ remain (want 0)')"`.

8. Final rebuild. Then run the deterministic validator and make sure it passes:
     python3 tools/check_conformance.py <out-from-manifest>

Work autonomously: run the tools, read their output, edit the module, rebuild, repeat. Do NOT hand-write the register JSON — the build pipeline generates it from the SVD + your curation.

When done, OUTPUT a concise report: final peripheral/register counts, the final provenance line (must be 0 TBD), every AUTO_PREFIX_OVERRIDE / CHAPTER_FALLBACK / ACCESS_FIX you added (with the reasoning), the SVD naming convention you observed, and the check_conformance result.

nodes.title: Curate hero peripherals + Tier 2
nodes.prompt:
You raised the STRUCTURAL register-map for this STM32 (see datasheets/{{chip}}/chip.json for the MPN and the datasheet PDF). Now RAISE FIDELITY on the peripherals people actually program, and add the Tier 2 parametric slice. The chip module is tools/chips/{{chip}}.py; the part JSON is the manifest's `out`.

A) HERO PERIPHERALS (verified access + real enums). Pick the handful most-programmed on this family: RCC, GPIO, the USART/UART, a general-purpose TIM, SPI, and ADC. For each, add a curated spec to the PERIPHERALS list of tools/chips/{{chip}}.py following the exact shape documented in tools/ADDING-A-CHIP.md (svd_name, description, section_keyfn or section_map, registers{access overrides}, fields{enums + access}, emit[...]). Read the real bit/enum meanings from the reference manual, do not invent them:
     python3 tools/rm_inspect.py datasheets/{{chip}}/<rm-pdf> RCC_CFGR1 --text   # shows the "00: .. 01: .." bit descriptions
Mirror how tools/chips/stm32g474.py wrote its RCC/GPIO/USART specs — but use THIS chip's sections, enums, and register names (U5 differs from G4: e.g. RCC register names/bits, GPIO is the same MODER pattern). Rebuild after each peripheral and confirm it still builds 0 TBD.

B) TIER 2 (electrical / limits) from the datasheet PDF (datasheets/{{chip}}/<ds-pdf>, doc id + rev are in the manifest). Hand-curate a HERO SLICE — do not attempt the whole datasheet:
     - LIMITS.absolute_maximum: VDD–VSS, VIN, storage/junction temperature.
     - LIMITS.recommended_operating: VDD range, operating temperature range.
     - ELECTRICAL: max core/AHB clock f_HCLK, and 1–2 key supply currents (Run, Stop).
   EVERY value needs a `conditions` object (even if it just states the mode/voltage/temperature) and a `provenance` citing the datasheet doc id + rev. Use `null` for any min/typ/max the datasheet does not state — never guess a number. Set TIERS=[1, 2] in the module.

Rebuild a final time (python3 tools/build.py {{chip}}) and run python3 tools/check_conformance.py <out-from-manifest> — it must stay green.

This step is best-effort quality polish: if a particular enum or value is unclear in the docs, leave it auto/null rather than guessing. OUTPUT a summary of which peripherals you curated, which enums you added, and the Tier 2 values you encoded (with their datasheet sections).

nodes.title: Register part in the MCP worker
nodes.prompt:
Register the freshly-encoded STM32 part so the OpenDatasheet MCP worker serves it. Read datasheets/{{chip}}/chip.json for the MPN and the `out` path (e.g. data/stm32u575zi.json).

1. Make the build:data script build this chip too. In package.json, the "build:data" script currently runs `python3 tools/build.py stm32g474`; append this chip's id so it builds both, e.g. `python3 tools/build.py stm32g474 {{chip}}`.
2. Register the part in src/lib.ts (read its top — it documents the exact pattern):
     - add an import: `import u575 from "../data/<out-basename>.json";` (use a sensible local name; the path is the manifest `out`).
     - add an entry to the PARTS map keyed by the EXACT MPN from the manifest, e.g. `"STM32U575ZI": u575 as Part,`.
   (No errata overlay for this part — leave ERRATA alone.)
3. Rebuild and typecheck:
     npm run build:data
     npm run typecheck      # tsc --noEmit — must be clean
4. Confirm the part JSON exists at the manifest `out` and the MPN now appears in the registry.

Do NOT deploy (no `npm run deploy`, no wrangler deploy) — registration + local build only. OUTPUT: confirm the package.json + src/lib.ts edits, that build:data and typecheck pass, and the final part JSON path + size.

nodes.title: Query the live MCP server
nodes.prompt:
Verify the newly-registered STM32 part is actually QUERYABLE through the OpenDatasheet MCP server (the whole point of the project), by running the worker locally and querying it. Read datasheets/{{chip}}/chip.json for the MPN (e.g. STM32U575ZI) and `out` (e.g. data/stm32u575zi.json → raw path /parts/stm32u575zi.json, lowercase).

1. Start the worker locally in the background on port 8787:
     npx wrangler dev --port 8787 >/tmp/wrangler-{{chip}}.log 2>&1 &
   Then POLL until it is ready (up to ~60s): loop `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" http://localhost:8787/` until it returns 200/426/405 (any response means it's up). If wrangler fails to start (check /tmp/wrangler-{{chip}}.log), say so and fall back to validating the JSON directly with jq/python, then SKIP to step 4.
2. Query via the MCP tools using the helper (tools/query.sh local <cmd> <MPN>):
     ./tools/query.sh local list                 # the MPN must appear in the list
     ./tools/query.sh local describe <MPN>        # must return the full part document, not an error
     ./tools/query.sh local raw /parts/<mpn-lowercase>.json   # the static raw route
   Confirm describe returns real content: it should include the register-map profile with peripherals like RCC and GPIO, the conformance tiers, and provenance. Pull out and show one concrete register (e.g. grep RCC_CR or a GPIO MODER) with its fields + provenance to prove the data is real and cited.
3. Kill the wrangler dev process you started (e.g. `kill %1` or pkill -f "wrangler dev").
4. OUTPUT: paste the key query results — the list_parts hit, a trimmed describe excerpt showing a real cited register, and the raw-route status — so it is evident the MCP serves this part end to end. If anything failed (worker wouldn't start, MPN missing, describe errored), report it clearly as a FAILURE.

nodes.title: Verify vs reference manual + datasheet
nodes.prompt:
You are the independent VERIFY step: cross-check that the encoded STM32 part faithfully matches its source reference manual + datasheet, beyond the structural validator. Read datasheets/{{chip}}/chip.json for the MPN, `out` path, and the RM/DS pdf names + doc ids + revisions.

Do these checks:
1. Re-run the deterministic validator and require it green:
     python3 tools/check_conformance.py <out-from-manifest>
2. REGISTER-LEVEL SPOT CHECK (the important part). Pick ~8 registers spread across DIFFERENT peripherals (include at least: an RCC clock register, a GPIO register, a USART register, a TIM register, an ADC status register, and any *ICR/*SCR clear register). For each, compare the ENCODED entry in the part JSON (its `access`, its `provenance.section`, and a field or two) against the reference manual:
     python3 tools/rm_inspect.py datasheets/{{chip}}/<rm-pdf> <REG>            # access tokens
     python3 tools/rm_inspect.py datasheets/{{chip}}/<rm-pdf> <REG> --text | head -60   # to read the section number + bit meanings
   Flag any MISMATCH: wrong access (e.g. a status/clear register encoded read-write when the RM says rc_w1 → should be w1c), a provenance.section that points at the wrong chapter, or an enum value that contradicts the RM.
3. TIER 2 SPOT CHECK (if the part declares tier 2): pick 1–2 electrical/limit values and confirm the number + unit + cited section match the datasheet (datasheets/{{chip}}/<ds-pdf>).

KNOWN PROJECT CONVENTIONS — DO NOT FLAG THESE AS DISCREPANCIES (they are correct per tools/ADDING-A-CHIP.md):
  - A CLEAR REGISTER (name ends ICR/SCR/IFCR/FCR/CLRFR, or whose RM access is shown as plain `w`) encoded as `w1c` (or `w0c`). ST marks write-1-to-clear registers as `w` in the RM, but `w1c`/`w0c` is the CORRECT, more-informative encoding — not an error.
  - A register-level `access` SUMMARY that differs from the RM WHEN the register's individual FIELDS are correctly typed. Consumers and check_conformance use field-level access; the register-level value is only a coarse summary. Only flag register-level access for a register that has NO fields.
Flag ONLY genuine FIELD-LEVEL errors: a status/data field whose access contradicts the RM (e.g. a status flag left `read-write` when the RM says `rc_w1`/`rc_w0` → should be `w1c`/`w0c`), or an enum value that contradicts the RM.

THEN WRITE YOUR FINDINGS to a gate file the next step reads:
   - Create the file build/verify-issues.txt (mkdir -p build first).
   - Write ONE LINE PER GENUINE FACTUAL DISCREPANCY you found (wrong access / wrong section / illegal or contradicted enum / wrong Tier-2 number). Be specific: "REG: encoded X, RM says Y".
   - If the encoding is faithful and you found NO genuine discrepancies, create build/verify-issues.txt EMPTY (e.g. `: > build/verify-issues.txt`). Do NOT write style nitpicks or "could be improved" notes — only real errors that make the data WRONG.

Finally, OUTPUT a human-readable verdict: which registers you checked, the evidence, and end with a line exactly of the form `VERDICT: PASS — <summary>` (if build/verify-issues.txt is empty) or `VERDICT: FAIL — <count> discrepancies` (if not).

args.command: test -f build/verify-issues.txt && test ! -s build/verify-issues.txt && echo "VERIFY GATE PASS: no discrepancies" || { echo "VERIFY GATE FAIL — discrepancies (or missing verify file):"; cat build/verify-issues.txt 2>/dev/null; exit 1; }
